Apollo 1. On January 27, 1967, a cabin fire broke out during a launch-pad test of the Apollo command module. The crew—Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee—were overcome by smoke and toxic fumes. They could not escape, and all three were killed.

Gus Grissom was a veteran Mercury and Gemini astronaut. Ed White had performed the first American spacewalk. Roger Chaffee was on his first spaceflight. Their loss was profound and transformative. The pure oxygen atmosphere in the command module, pressurized at higher than normal levels during the test, fed the fire and made escape impossible. Investigations revealed that the Apollo capsule's design had numerous flaws: faulty wiring, flammable materials, and a hatch that could not be opened quickly from inside.

The disaster halted the Apollo program for 21 months. During that time, NASA undertook a complete redesign of the command module and crew safety protocols. The capsule's hatch was replaced with an outward-opening hatch that could be jettisoned in seconds. The changes made to Apollo in the aftermath of this tragedy would eventually enable the moon landings that followed. The three astronauts' sacrifice was not forgotten; their deaths forced a reckoning with the risks of space exploration and led to safer spacecraft design practices.
